title: Rockaway Traditional Land
summary: Rockaway preserves a Native name on the shores of a much older Lenape homeland. Bays, islands and waterways connected people before colonial deeds and settlement divided the land. Displacement did not end Lenape life: communities continue in the homeland and in nations beyond New York. Honoring Rockaway means connecting the familiar name to that living history, while treating particular family relationships with care.
why_this_matters: Rockaway Traditional Land presents western Long Island, Jamaica Bay, Hempstead Bay, and the south shore islands as Native homeland. It connects early records with waterways, coastal movement, and the continued importance of public memory.
introduction_title: Rockaway within a living Lenape homeland
introduction_content:
The colonial records below connect Rockaway people with Jamaica Bay, South Shore lands and neighboring Native leaders. Those documents capture negotiations and colonial claims; they do not define the whole life of a community. National Park Service research places Rockaway within the broader Lenape history of western Long Island.

Lenape Center describes a people whose present-day nations and cultural work extend across a diaspora as well as the ancestral homeland. Displacement can separate a community from land without ending its relationship to that land. This is a broader Lenape connection, not a claim that a particular living nation contains every Rockaway descendant. Acknowledgment here should make room for those living voices and for the responsibilities carried by a name that survived the growth of the modern city.

Sources for ancestry and continuance: National Park Service; Lenape Center. See References for citations and the historical sources used below.
history_content:
Early colonial sources describe Rockaway villages, south shore waterways, and involvement in Hempstead-area land records. Rockaway history overlaps with Merrick, Massapequa, Canarsie, and other western Long Island communities through diplomacy, trade, kinship, and colonial pressure.

Named-source moments include the 1639 western Long Island deed boundary reaching from Rockaway, the 1643 Hempstead deed context linking Rockaway with Massapequa and Merrick-related communities, the 1655 Rockaway Neck deed naming Ruckquaheag, Ronnessoke/Suscaneman, Adam/Achitteronose, and others, and the 1657 Hempstead conference naming Mangwobe of Rockaway with Tackapousha, Wyandanch, Cockenoe, and Merrick representatives. [1. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700.; William Wallace Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent (1911).; Documents Relative to the Colonial History of the State of New York, vol. XIV.]

On April 25, 1671, a Hempstead town meeting banned any inhabitant from plowing or breaking up planting land for Native people, or helping them do it. It sent John Hicks, George Hewlett and John Jackson to Rockaway to warn away all Native people except those who "do really belong to that place," and ordered about forty acres laid out for planting corn for the Rockaway families, "being about ten," as the governor had ordered. Records of the Towns of North and South Hempstead, vol. I, printed p. 276

Village and archaeological references are kept broad so sensitive places are not mapped for visitation.
geometry_cleanup_notes: The illustrated southeast wedge between Canarsie and Merrick, focused on eastern Jamaica Bay, southern Queens, and the Rockaway Peninsula without extending into western Jamaica Bay land assigned to Canarsie in the reference-guided display. The transition toward Merrick and Canarsie is generalized across modern shoreline land pieces.
